science.title: Greenland meltwater adds to AMOC weakening, but updated model finds no tipping point in sight
science.description: The state of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) has been a hot topic among climate scientists in recent years. The AMOC is crucial for climate regulation because it pulls warm surface water from the tropics north and sends colder, deeper water south, redistributing large amounts of heat, helping to sustain marine ecosystems and keeping global weather patterns steady. However, most standard AMOC-focused climate models may be missing an important piece of the puzzle—they don't include the growing pulse of freshwater from Greenland ice melt, which could further disrupt the AMOC.

science.description: A predicted solar storm delivered a spectacular show over Alberta skies this week, with northern lights visible across Airdrie, Rocky View County and communities throughout the province. When that material reaches Earth, it can trigger geomagnetic activity and produce auroras. A forecast that delivered NOAA’s Space Weather Prediction Center said the CME was expected to affect Earth and could lead to moderate storm levels, depending on the orientation of the embedded magnetic field. googletag.cmd.push(function() { if($(document).width()<900) { s = googletag.defineSlot('/50748803/dai-all-bigbox', [300, 250], 'div-gpt-1642457838145-bbm4'); s.setTargeting('URL', [window.location.pathname]); s.setTargeting('position', [1642457838145]) s.setTargeting('story_id', 'solar-storm-lights-up-alberta-skies-as-northern-lights-dazzle-airdrie-area-residents'); s.addService(googletag.pubads()); googletag.pubads().refresh([s], {changeCorrelator: false}); } }); The agency said auroras could become visible over some northern and upper Midwest states, from New York to Idaho. Ratzlaff wrote that KP6/G2 or greater auroras can be visible overhead and possibly under urban skies in Alberta, while KP7/G3 or greater displays can stretch across the entire sky. googletag.cmd.push(function() { if($(document).width()<900) { s = googletag.defineSlot('/50748803/dai-all-bigbox', [300, 250], 'div-gpt-1642457838145-bbm6'); s.setTargeting('URL', [window.location.pathname]); s.setTargeting('position', [1642457838145]) s.setTargeting('story_id', 'solar-storm-lights-up-alberta-skies-as-northern-lights-dazzle-airdrie-area-residents'); s.addService(googletag.pubads()); googletag.pubads().refresh([s], {changeCorrelator: false}); } }); Full Sky Alberta Aurora Possible, July 2 by Chris Ratzlaff Possibility of Full Sky Alberta Aurora, July 2 +/-24hrs Read on Substack What causes the northern lights? According to the Canadian Space Agency, the northern lights, or aurora borealis, are colourful displays of light seen in the night sky in the northern hemisphere. The southern hemisphere has its own version, known as the southern lights, or aurora australis. Auroras form when the sun sends charged particles, including electrons and protons, into space through the solar wind. googletag.cmd.push(function() { if($(document).width()<900) { s = googletag.defineSlot('/50748803/dai-all-bigbox', [300, 250], 'div-gpt-1642457838145-bbm7'); s.setTargeting('URL', [window.location.pathname]); s.setTargeting('position', [1642457838145]) s.setTargeting('story_id', 'solar-storm-lights-up-alberta-skies-as-northern-lights-dazzle-airdrie-area-residents'); s.addService(googletag.pubads()); googletag.pubads().refresh([s], {changeCorrelator: false}); } }); Earth’s magnetic field redirects much of that solar wind around the planet, but magnetic field lines can stretch and snap back, sending charged particles toward Earth’s upper atmosphere. When those particles collide with gases high above the surface, they produce tiny flashes of light. googletag.cmd.push(function() { if($(document).width()<900) { s = googletag.defineSlot('/50748803/dai-all-bigbox', [300, 250], 'div-gpt-1642457838145-bbm8'); s.setTargeting('URL', [window.location.pathname]); s.setTargeting('position', [1642457838145]) s.setTargeting('story_id', 'solar-storm-lights-up-alberta-skies-as-northern-lights-dazzle-airdrie-area-residents'); s.addService(googletag.pubads()); googletag.pubads().refresh([s], {changeCorrelator: false}); } }); As billions of those flashes occur in sequence, the aurora can appear to ripple, shimmer or dance across the sky. Why the colours change The Canadian Space Agency says aurora colours depend on several factors, including the gases in Earth’s atmosphere, the altitude of the aurora, atmospheric density and the energy involved. Green is the most common colour seen from the ground and is produced when charged particles collide with oxygen molecules at altitudes of about 100 to 300 kilometres. Pink and dark red can appear along the lower edge of an aurora when electrons strike nitrogen molecules around 100 kilometres above the ground. Red auroras are produced higher in the atmosphere, around 300 to 400 kilometres, when charged particles collide with oxygen atoms. googletag.cmd.push(function() { if($(document).width()<900) { s = googletag.defineSlot('/50748803/dai-all-bigbox', [300, 250], 'div-gpt-1642457838145-bbm9'); s.setTargeting('URL', [window.location.pathname]); s.setTargeting('position', [1642457838145]) s.setTargeting('story_id', 'solar-storm-lights-up-alberta-skies-as-northern-lights-dazzle-airdrie-area-residents'); s.addService(googletag.pubads()); googletag.pubads().refresh([s], {changeCorrelator: false}); } }); Blue and purple auroras can be produced by hydrogen and helium molecules, though those colours can be harder for the human eye to see against the night sky. Local skies, local photos Across Airdrie and the surrounding area, residents captured the aurora from back roads, fields, parks and neighbourhoods. Many photos showed vivid green bands stretching across the horizon, while others captured pink and purple pillars reaching overhead. googletag.cmd.push(function() { if($(document).width()<900) { s = googletag.defineSlot('/50748803/dai-all-bigbox', [300, 250], 'div-gpt-1642457838145-bbm10'); s.setTargeting('URL', [window.location.pathname]); s.setTargeting('position', [1642457838145]) s.setTargeting('story_id', 'solar-storm-lights-up-alberta-skies-as-northern-lights-dazzle-airdrie-area-residents'); s.addService(googletag.pubads()); googletag.pubads().refresh([s], {changeCorrelator: false}); } }); The display also drew widespread attention on social media, where local residents compared viewing locations, camera settings and favourite shots from the night. googletag.cmd.push(function() { if($(document).width()<900) { s = googletag.defineSlot('/50748803/dai-all-bigbox', [300, 250], 'div-gpt-1642457838145-bbm11'); s.setTargeting('URL', [window.location.pathname]); s.setTargeting('position', [1642457838145]) s.setTargeting('story_id', 'solar-storm-lights-up-alberta-skies-as-northern-lights-dazzle-airdrie-area-residents'); s.addService(googletag.pubads()); googletag.pubads().refresh([s], {changeCorrelator: false}); } }); How to get the best view The Canadian Space Agency says auroras are generally easier to see away from light pollution, where city lights do not wash out low-intensity displays. Clear skies also matter. Clouds, precipitation and bright moonlight can make auroras harder to see. The agency says auroras often appear a few hours after sunset and tend to become more intense around midnight. Viewers are also encouraged to look all around the sky, not only north, because auroras can appear in different directions during stronger displays. Ratzlaff’s aurora-chasing guidance also reminds viewers to drive carefully, park fully off the road, stay off private property and be considerate of others when using headlights near viewing areas. googletag.cmd.push(function() { if($(document).width()<900) { s = googletag.defineSlot('/50748803/dai-all-bigbox', [300, 250], 'div-gpt-1642457838145-bbm12'); s.setTargeting('URL', [window.location.pathname]); s.setTargeting('position', [1642457838145]) s.setTargeting('story_id', 'solar-storm-lights-up-alberta-skies-as-northern-lights-dazzle-airdrie-area-residents'); s.addService(googletag.pubads()); googletag.pubads().refresh([s], {changeCorrelator: false}); } }); A shared Alberta sky For many residents, the event became more than a forecast. It was a memorable summer night when people across the region stepped outside, looked up and saw the same colours moving above them.
